reports.title: SMS Holdout Test

items.lab: less revenue, and not statistically significant

spent on SMS across the 38-day test, for no measurable lift

blocks.html:
What we found

SMS isn't adding revenue we wouldn't already be getting.

We split the account in half. One half got SMS in every automated flow. The other half got zero SMS, email only. Everything else stayed identical.

After 38 days, the SMS half brought in 1.98% less revenue than the no-SMS half. That gap isn't statistically meaningful, so the honest read is no effect either way. What it rules out is a big win: at 95% confidence, the most SMS could be adding is about 1.3%.

The revenue Klaviyo credits to SMS is largely revenue email was already going to capture.

blocks.cap: 38-day total attributed revenue, A$. The SMS-on group came in 1.98% lower.

Is the difference statistically significant? No. Purchase rate 2.675% vs 2.714%, p = 0.31. The confidence range runs from −0.11 to +0.04 percentage points, which straddles zero. A separate day-by-day revenue test agreed (p = 0.13). Two methods, same answer.

Basket size was unaffected. AOV differs by 46 cents, p = 0.72. Whatever small gap exists is fewer orders, not smaller ones.

blocks.html:
A second finding worth your attention

36% of revenue converts before any marketing message can reach it.

We checked 460 orders across the test window. Over half were placed within an hour of the customer's profile being created. One in five within a single minute.

blocks.cap: Share of orders. 52% happen before any message sends.
blocks.title: Time from first visit to order

blocks.html:
For that first half, the buyer had not opted in yet, so they were on no list and no automation could reach them: no welcome email had sent, no abandoned cart had fired, no SMS had gone out. The site, the ads and the offer did the work.

So the business splits cleanly:

  • ~36% of revenue: same-session conversion. Acquisition territory, not retention.
  • ~64% of revenue: the population retention marketing can actually influence. This is where the holdout ran, and where SMS showed nothing.

One more thing

Repeat buying was low in both groups over the 38-day window (about 1.003 orders per buyer). We'd flag it as an area worth watching, though a longer window would measure returning-customer behaviour far better than a 38-day test can.

What we'd do next

  • Hold SMS spend where it is. No evidence supports scaling it. The ceiling on any benefit is about 1.3%, and SMS costs real money per send.
  • Keep the test running. Hold the holdout live at this pace for roughly another two months, to be sure there's no slower, carry-on benefit from SMS that a 38-day window would miss. If SMS is worth anything, a longer run will surface it; if it isn't, we'll know with more certainty.
  • Look at repeat purchase separately. There may be room to lift returning-customer rate, but that deserves its own analysis over a longer period rather than a conclusion from this test.

Every profile was randomly assigned to one of two groups, locked at assignment. Every SMS in every live flow was gated to fire only for the treatment group. We audited all 26 live flows to confirm no message leaked to the control group, including three flows edited mid-test.

Groups landed at 353,109 and 353,380, a near-perfect split.

On the numbers: revenue, orders, buyers and AOV are exact, pulled from the full account. The 36% same-session figure comes from a 460-order sample, so treat it as close rather than precise.

What this test doesn't tell us: whether SMS influences a first-time purchase. Those orders happen before anyone is measurable. This measures SMS among customers we can actually reach.

reports.summary: SMS shows no measurable revenue lift.
